Content:
Suppose we are given the equation [MATH: \log_3 x = 4.] Can we determine [MATH: x?]

Content:
Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate [MATH: x,] we must exponentiate both sides of this equation.

Content:
The base of the logarithm is [MATH: 3,] so we use a base of [MATH: 3] for the exponentiation as well:
[MATH: \log_{3} x|= 4; 3^{(\log_{3} x)}|= 3^{4}]

Content:
The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: 3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.] Therefore, we get

Content:
[MATH: x|= 3^{4}; x|= 81.]

Content:
We conclude that [MATH: x = 81] is the solution.

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \log_7 (2x + 1) = 1,] then what is [MATH: x?]

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is [MATH: 7,] so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

[MATH: \log_{7} (2x + 1)|= 1; 7^{\log_{7} (2x + 1)}|= 7^{1}]

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: 7^{\log_7 (2x + 1)} = 2x+1.]

Therefore, we get

[MATH: 2x + 1|= 7; 2x|= 6; x|= 3.]

sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: 2\log_5 (x-3)+1 = 5,] then what is the value of [MATH: x?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we make [MATH: \log_5 (x-3)] the subject of the equation by moving everything else to the right-hand side. This gives

[MATH: 2\log_{5} (x − 3) + 1|= 5; 2\log_{5} (x − 3)|= 4; \log_{5} (x − 3)|= 2.]

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is [MATH: 5,] so we use a base of [MATH: 5] for the exponentiation as well:

[MATH: \log_{5} (x − 3)|= 2; 5^{\log_{5} (x − 3)}|= 5^{2}]

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that [MATH: 5^{\log_5 (x - 3)} = x-3.]

Therefore, we get

[MATH: x − 3|= 5^{2}; x − 3|= 25; x|= 28]

Therefore, we get
